user.title: Battery Management
user.description: Pick the household grid-power sensor (+ = import, - = export) and how many battery units to coordinate. You can tune the control parameters later under Configure.

data_description.grid_power_sensor: The household meter this steers on. Positive must mean importing, negative exporting. Everything else is derived from this one reading.
data_description.unit_count: How many packs to coordinate. Each gets its own screen next.
data_description.bias: Aim for this much import instead of exactly zero, so a brief overshoot still exports nothing.
data_description.deadband: Ignore errors smaller than this, otherwise the packs chase every kettle. Costs a steady-state error of at most bias + deadband.
data_description.kp: How hard it corrects per tick: new setpoint = old + Kp x error. Higher reacts faster and overshoots sooner. 0.25 at 15 s is proven stable here.
data_description.interval: Seconds between decisions. Do not go below 15: the Modbus sensors lag 10-30 s, and at 10 s both packs wound up and discharged into an export.
data_description.min_output: Below this the packs are told to do nothing at all. It floors the total, not only each pack's share, so a small demand is never split into two amounts neither pack can hold accurately - the packs' own firmware warns when it gets one. Releases again at three quarters of this value, so a setpoint resting near the line cannot switch them on and off every tick. The setpoint keeps integrating meanwhile, so a persistent small import still climbs over the floor on its own. Measure it for your hardware.
data_description.unit_max: Hard ceiling per pack, needed because the target entity's own maximum is unreliable - one unit here reports 10000 for a 3500 W device.

unit_device.title: Battery unit {index} of {total}: pick the device
unit_device.description: Pick the Anker device for this unit and the next screen is filled in for you - you still get to check it. Leave it empty to select all six entities by hand.

data_description.device_id: Pick the device and the next screen is filled in for you, for review. Leave empty to choose all six entities by hand.

unit.title: Battery unit {index} of {total}
unit.description: Select the Modbus control entities for this Anker SOLIX Max AC unit. The two limit fields are optional and expect a percentage - leave them blank to use 100 % / 5 %.

data_description.name: Used in this integration's own sensor names. Must be unique: two packs sharing a name would be treated as one.
data_description.operating_mode_select: The select that switches this pack between its own control and being driven from outside. Which option means what is asked on the next screen.
data_description.grid_flow_select: The select that chooses charging or discharging. Must offer charge and discharge literally - those are written as-is.
data_description.target_power_number: The number this pack's share of the setpoint is written to. Always positive; the direction comes from the flow select.
data_description.soc_sensor: Drives the split between packs and every SoC limit. A pack whose state of charge cannot be read is skipped entirely.
data_description.charge_limit_number: The pack's own upper limit, as a percentage. Leave empty to assume 100 %. Never point this at a watt entity.
data_description.discharge_limit_number: The pack's own lower limit. Leave empty to assume 5 %. This is the hardware backstop the coordinator stays above.
data_description.unit_phase: Which leg of the supply this pack is on: 1, 2 or 3. Leave it at 0 and it is measured. Anything you type here wins over any measurement - if you have read the meter cupboard, you know better than a probe does.
data_description.power_sensor: The pack's own power reading. Never used for control - it lags 10-30 s - but it is what lets the trace show what the pack actually did next to what it was told to do.
data_description.charge_power_sensor: The pack's own charging power, in watts. Optional, and never used for control - it is what lets the integration count how much energy went in and how much of it was bought rather than caught. No sensor, no energy figures; nothing is guessed.

unit_modes.title: Battery unit: {name} - what its modes mean
unit_modes.description:
This unit offers: {options}.

Pick which one hands control to the coordinator, and which one gives it back when you switch off. Leave the second empty if there is nothing to return to - the unit is then simply commanded 0 W, which is a safe resting state. A pack without its own P1 meter has no self-consumption mode, so this is normal.

data.mode_safe: Option to return to when switching off

data_description.mode_control: The option this pack must be set to before it will take orders. Usually third_party_control.
data_description.mode_safe: Where it is put when you switch off or Home Assistant unloads. Leave empty for a pack with no meter of its own: it is then simply commanded 0 W and its mode left alone, which is a safe resting state.

error.duplicate_name: Another unit already uses this name. Names must be unique, otherwise the two packs are treated as one.
error.duplicate_entity: This entity is already used for another field on this unit. Each field needs its own entity.
error.limit_not_percentage: This looks like a power entity, not a state-of-charge percentage. The limit fields expect a percentage (0-100); leave blank to use 100 % / 5 %.
error.missing_options: This select does not offer the options the coordinator needs (self_consumption / third_party_control, or charge / discharge). Check the entity, or adjust the option strings in const.py if your firmware renamed them.

tuning.title: Tune the coordinator
tuning.description: Saving reloads the integration. Each unit is briefly released as far as it can be, then the coordinator resumes on its own with the setpoint it had.

data.fast_charge_hold: Keep the packs full after a fast charge
data.full_charge_minutes: Minutes from empty to full at max power
data.external_timeout: Minutes an external setpoint stays valid
data.discharge_recovery: Charge back this far before discharging again (%)

data_description.bias: Aim for this much import instead of exactly zero, so a brief overshoot still exports nothing.
data_description.deadband: Ignore errors smaller than this, otherwise the packs chase every kettle. Costs a steady-state error of at most bias + deadband.
data_description.kp: How hard it corrects per tick: new setpoint = old + Kp x error. Higher reacts faster and overshoots sooner. 0.25 at 15 s is proven stable here.
data_description.interval: Seconds between decisions. Do not go below 15: the Modbus sensors lag 10-30 s, and at 10 s both packs wound up and discharged into an export.
data_description.min_output: Below this the packs are told to do nothing at all. It floors the total, not only each pack's share, so a small demand is never split into two amounts neither pack can hold accurately - the packs' own firmware warns when it gets one. Releases again at three quarters of this value, so a setpoint resting near the line cannot switch them on and off every tick. data_description.unit_max: Hard ceiling per pack, needed because the target entity's own maximum is unreliable - one unit here reports 10000 for a 3500 W device.
data_description.fast_charge_hold: On: the switch stays on at full and holds them there until you release it. Off: it switches itself off and your mode discharges them again.
data_description.full_charge_minutes: Measured once, per pack. Gives both the minutes-to-full estimate and the usable capacity that the solar-aware charge ceiling needs. 0 hides both rather than guessing.
data_description.external_timeout: In External plan mode: if no new plan arrives within this time, control returns to following the meter instead of freezing on the last instruction.
data_description.discharge_recovery: Once a pack has been emptied it waits until it is this many points above its floor before it discharges again. Without it, the sun lifting a pack from 5 % to 6 % gets discharged straight back to 5 %, over and over - and the bottom of the pack is the worst place to cycle it. Counted above the floor, so it follows your SoC reserve and each pack's own discharge limit. It never blocks charging, and a pack coming down from full still empties all the way to its limit. 0 switches it off.
data_description.kp_return: How fast the command is wound back down. Higher than the gain above on purpose: coming back cannot oscillate, and it is what stops the packs exporting into a load that has already gone away. Set it equal to the gain above for the old symmetric behaviour.
data_description.trace: One CSV row per tick under config/battery_management_trace/, so a question about last week can still be answered. Costs about 2 MB a day.
data_description.trace_days: Whole days older than this are deleted.
data_description.grid_max_age: Stop regulating once the meter has not reported for this long, instead of integrating a number that stopped moving. A frozen reading stays perfectly readable, so nothing else notices it: the setpoint walks to full discharge and holds there. 0 trusts the reading whatever its age.

dynamic.title: Dynamic tariff
dynamic.description: Optional. Without a price sensor the Dynamic mode is not offered and nothing else changes. Exchange (day-ahead) prices are enough: tax and markup shift every hour equally, so the cheap-to-expensive order is the same.

data.cheap_hours: Hours a day to buy on
data.charge_below_soc: Only buy below this state of charge (%)
data.solar_forecast_max: Fallback: skip buying above this many kWh expected
data.expensive_hours: Hours a day to save the charge for

data_description.price_source: Fetching them ourselves saves installing a second custom integration, which matters at a house you do not live in. Frank Energie publishes its market prices openly, so no login is needed - and the price used is the all-in one, including tax and markup, not the bare exchange price. Pick the sensor option for any other supplier: Nord Pool, ENTSO-e, EnergyZero, Tibber and the rest are all read by shape.
data_description.cheap_hours: How many of the coming day's cheapest slots may be used to charge from the grid. Ranked over a rolling 24 hours, not over everything published.
data_description.charge_below_soc: Fallback ceiling, used only while the charge time is unmeasured. Once it is, the solar-aware ceiling replaces it.
data_description.solar_forecast_max: Only used while the charge time is unmeasured, since without a capacity there is no way to turn kWh into a percentage. 0 ignores the forecast.
data_description.expensive_hours: Outside the dearest hours the packs do not discharge, so a cheap hour is bought from the grid and the stored kWh go to the peak instead. 0 switches this off.
data_description.discharge_anyway_soc: A pack this full discharges even during a cheap hour. Refusing would leave nowhere for the sun still coming, and spilling free energy to save a few cents is a bad trade.
data_description.solar_forecast_sensors: Pick every roof plane; they are summed. Prefer the 'remaining today' variants - a whole-day total is right at 02:00 and wrong at 17:00.
data_description.solar_produced_sensor: Only needed if the sensors above give a day total: this is subtracted, leaving what is still to come.
data_description.price_resolution: The market settles in 15-minute blocks and suppliers are starting to publish that way. Taking the feed as published is the more precise choice - the coordinator will happily buy on a single cheap quarter. By the hour is easier to read: 24 bars on a chart instead of 96, at the cost of averaging away the peaks inside each hour. Whichever you pick applies to the decisions and the chart alike, so they can never disagree.
data_description.price_margin: Only buy from the grid when the hour is at least this much per kWh cheaper than the dear hours it is saving for. Covers the round-trip loss (~12%) plus wear, and stops "cheapest three hours left" from calling the most expensive hour of the day cheap. 0 = pure ranking.

shadow.title: Shadow running
shadow.description: Only matters while Dry run is on. Simulating the meter is what makes a shadow comparison honest: without it the other controller is already regulating the meter, so this one sees nothing to do and parks at zero.

data.shadow_simulate: Simulate the meter from reconstructed demand

data_description.shadow_simulate: Only matters in dry run. Without it the other controller is already regulating the meter, so this one sees nothing to do and parks at zero - comparing the old system with itself.
data_description.battery_power_sensor: Signed, + discharging, for both packs together. Leave empty and it is read back from the target entities, where the other controller writes. Never the grid meter: the reconstruction adds the two together.

phases.title: Fuse protection per phase
phases.description:
The packs are single-phase and the control loop only knows the household total. A pack charging at 3500 W on a leg that is already pulling 20 A takes that leg to 35 A - while the other two sit half idle and the total looks perfectly reasonable.

Point this at your meter's per-phase power sensors, in L1, L2, L3 order, and each leg gets its own ceiling. Leave the list empty and none of this exists.

Which pack sits on which leg is measured, not configured: one pack is asked to move while the others hold still, and whichever leg moves with it is the answer.

data.phase_detect: Find out which pack is on which phase

data_description.phase_power_sensors: In L1, L2, L3 order - the order decides which leg is which. Signed like the main meter: + import, - export. Empty switches the whole protection off. One sensor means a single-phase supply, and then everything is on that one leg.
data_description.phase_limit_amps: What your main fuse is rated at per phase, typically 25 or 35 in the Netherlands. Read it off the fuse itself rather than off your contract.
data_description.phase_voltage: Only used to turn the fuse rating into watts. 230 unless you know otherwise.
data_description.phase_margin: Left unused, for the kettle somebody switches on while we are deciding. Ten per cent of 25 A is 2.5 A of room. A fuse is not a cliff, but running it to the last ampere leaves nothing for the rest of the house.
data_description.phase_detect: Nothing in the Modbus data says how the cables were run, so it is measured: one pack is commanded while the others hold at 0, and the leg that moves with it is the answer. Takes about a minute per pack, during which the packs do not regulate. Switch it off if you would rather type the phases in yourself on each unit's page.
data_description.phase_redetect: On by default: an integration that has been down cannot vouch for what changed while it was. Switch it off once the wiring is known and stable - otherwise every restart parks the packs for a minute.
data_description.phase_probe_seconds: How long one pack is held at power before the legs are read. Longer is more reliable and more disruptive; the packs take a few seconds to respond and the meter a few more.

price_entity.title: Which price sensor
price_entity.description:
Any sensor that publishes upcoming prices will do. The shapes are recognised rather than the integrations, so changing supplier means pointing this somewhere else.

Leave it empty and Dynamic mode is simply not offered; everything else keeps working exactly as it does now.

data_description.price_sensor: Its attributes must hold a list of upcoming prices - most integrations publish one under `prices`, `raw_today` or similar. A shape that is not recognised gives an empty forecast, which disables buying rather than guessing at a price. Exchange prices are fine: tax and markup shift every hour equally, so the cheap-to-expensive order does not change.

error.duplicate_name: Another unit already uses this name. Names must be unique, otherwise the two packs are treated as one.
error.duplicate_entity: This entity is already used for another field on this unit. Each field needs its own entity.
error.limit_not_percentage: This looks like a power entity, not a state-of-charge percentage. The limit fields expect a percentage (0-100); leave blank to use 100 % / 5 %.
error.missing_options: This select does not offer the options the coordinator needs (self_consumption / third_party_control, or charge / discharge). Check the entity, or adjust the option strings in const.py if your firmware renamed them.
error.battery_power_is_grid: That is the grid meter, not the batteries. The reconstruction adds the two together, so using the meter here counts it twice and the comparison becomes worthless. Leave this empty unless you have a sensor for the packs' own combined power - empty reads it back from the target entities, which is what you want.
error.phase_sensor_is_grid: That is the whole-house meter, not one phase. A total cannot show a single leg sitting at 25 A, which is the only thing this protects against - and one sensor means “single-phase supply”, so a 25 A limit would land on your whole connection. Pick the per-phase sensors instead, usually named ..._phase_1, ..._phase_2, ..._phase_3.

state.external_stale: External plan went quiet, regulating on its own
state.dynamic_hold: Holding the charge for dearer hours
state.solar_headroom: Not buying, the sun still fits
state.phase_limit: Held back by the main fuse
state.phase_detect: Measuring which pack is on which phase
state.recovering: Charging back up before it discharges again

state.gave_up: Could not measure it; type it in

external_no_plan.title: Smart charging needs an external optimiser
external_no_plan.description:
The coordinator is set to **External plan**, but no plan has arrived in the last {timeout} minutes, so it has handed control back to normal grid-zero regulation.

This mode does not plan anything itself. It executes a plan produced elsewhere — typically **EMHASS**, which optimises against price, solar and load forecasts. EMHASS is a separate project: it is **not** installed with this integration and is not a dependency.

Install and configure it (or any other optimiser), and have it call the `battery_management.set_setpoint` service. Positive discharges, negative charges. This message clears itself as soon as a plan arrives.

Not using an optimiser? Pick a different mode — **Follow the meter** charges from your solar surplus and discharges on demand, with no extra software.

hand_back_impossible.title: {unit} cannot be handed back to {mode}
hand_back_impossible.description:
**{unit}** is set to return to `{mode}` when the coordinator is switched off or Home Assistant unloads. That pack does not offer that option — it only offers: {options}.

The command would simply be refused, and these packs have no watchdog: one would keep running its last instruction indefinitely, which is exactly what the safe revert exists to prevent. Dry run never reveals this, because nothing is written.

A pack without its own P1 meter has no self-consumption mode at all. For that one, **leave the hand-back empty**: it is then commanded 0 W and its mode is left alone, which is a safe resting state.

Fix it under **Configure → Battery unit entities**, walking through to the screen that asks what this unit's modes mean.

write_not_acknowledged.title: {units} is not acknowledging commands
write_not_acknowledged.description:
The coordinator has been writing to **{units}** for over {seconds} seconds without the pack ever showing the value back.

Commands are sent without waiting for a reply, so a refused write raises where nobody is listening. These packs also have no watchdog: one that stops accepting orders keeps running whatever it accepted last, indefinitely.

Check that the Anker integration is still connected and that the target entity is not disabled or read-only. This clears itself as soon as a command is acknowledged.

options.none: No prices (Dynamic mode is not offered)
options.frank_energie: Frank Energie — fetched directly, no account needed

options.published: As the supplier publishes them (quarter-hourly if they do)
